newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bunds torn lower by declining U.S. market.
newsitem.headline: Bunds torn lower by declining U.S. market.

text.p: German Bunds fell to heavy losses on Thursday as fresh economic data added to concern that U.S. economic activity was gaining pace.

March Bund futures fell as low as 99.30, down 1.54 points from their close on the last trading day, Monday December 30, and the yield on the benchmark 10-year Bund rose to 6.00 percent, up from 5.77 percent late on Monday.

Bunds had opened sharply lower and hovered around 100.00 for most of the session in reaction to a sharp fall in U.S. Treasuries on Tuesday following news of a strong gains in single-family home sales and consumer confidence.

But Treasuries tumbled after news on Thursday that a widely watched index of manufacturing activity, the National Association of Purchasing Managers (NAPM) Index rose to 54.0 in December from 52.7 in November.
A reading above 50 points to growth in manufacturing, while one below that level indicates contraction.
Stock and bond prices fell after the report, which apparently worried some investors that stronger economic growth might lead to a pickup in inflation and higher interest rates.
While Bunds outperformed Treasuries after the news, they were unable to escape sharp losses.
That scotched analysts' recent predictions that the German debt market rally would continue into 1997.

"The subject of inflation is back on the agenda in the U.S. and we're seeing a trend towards a reassessment of economic fundamentals there," said Werner Kraemer, market strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Frankfurt.

Kraemer predicted Bunds would continue to outperform U.S. bonds because economic fundamentals in Germany were more favourable to the debt market. He said the market was likely to be supported at the current six percent yield in 10-year bonds, an attractive level for investors.

But Kraemer added that in the current environment this month's issue of up to 25 billion marks of new 10-year paper -- the first fresh 10-year Bund issued since last April -- could put additional pressure on the market.
The traditional bank bond consortium meets on January 7 to set terms for up to 15 billion marks of new paper.
The bond will be topped up by up to 10 billion marks in the third 10 days of January.
